W2-LO1 - FPR Stepwise Approach

Technique Recipe

Explain and demonstrate the stepwise approach to Facilitated Positional Release (FPR).

Board-safe definition

Facilitated positional release is a passive, indirect OMM technique. The segment/tissue is placed in neutral/idling, a facilitating force is added, then the tissue is moved into its position of ease.

  1. Diagnose and monitor. Name the dysfunction and keep a palpating hand on the segment, tender tissue, or AGR.
  2. Place in neutral/idling. For spinal units, neutral means the facets are free to move, neither opened nor closed. In the cervical spine, course lab emphasizes flexing down to the level to create this idling position.
  3. Add the facilitating force. Usually use gentle compression or torsion. Use traction when compression is not tolerated or when the region makes traction more sensible.
  4. Move into ease. Position the segment into the freedom of motion. This is the indirect component.
  5. Hold, return, recheck. Hold for 3-5 seconds, passively return to anatomic neutral, repeat if needed, then reassess TART/motion.

Q: A patient has C5 ERSl. For FPR, do you begin in C5 ERSl or begin by placing the cervical unit in neutral/idling?

Answer

Begin by placing the cervical unit in neutral/idling, then add compression, then move into the ease of the dysfunction. Starting in the diagnosis/ease is the Still order, not the FPR order.

W2-LO2 - FPR/Still Indications, Contraindications, MOA

Technique Safety and Mechanism

State the indications, contraindications, and mechanism of action of FPR and Still Techniques.

Indications

  • Somatic dysfunction with restricted motion, TART, or local AGR.
  • Hypertonic muscles: superficial/group curve or deep/segmental restriction.
  • Fascial restrictions and patients with limited ROM who may tolerate low-force positioning.

Contraindications and Cautions

  • Patient cannot tolerate the treatment position or refuses treatment.
  • Recent trauma, unstable joint pathology, severe osteoporosis, malignancy, infection, severe rheumatologic disease, congenital instability/malformation, or stenosis.
  • Region-specific: cervical radiculopathy is a caution; hip replacement can contraindicate some lumbar leg-sweep setups.
TechniqueProposed MOAPractical implication
FPRShortens involved muscle spindles, decreases gamma efferent gain, lowers Ia afferent excitation, reduces extrafusal muscle tone.Use relaxed/passive patient positioning. Do not fight tone; shorten and quiet it.
StillUses the same proposed neurophysiologic relaxation, then adds a direct mobilizing arc through neutral toward the barrier.Start gentle and indirect, then carry the tissue into the direct phase while staying within physiologic ROM.
Force choice is clinical reasoning

Compression is common, but if compression worsens symptoms or jams the region, use traction/distraction or a smaller arc.

Q: Why can FPR and Still both be reasonable for a patient with low ROM?

Answer

Both can start from a tolerated, low-force position and can be kept within the patient's physiologic range. Still needs extra caution because it includes a direct component toward the barrier.

W2-LO3 - FPR vs Strain-Counterstrain

Technique Comparison

Compare and contrast FPR with Strain-Counterstrain Technique.

FeatureFPRStrain-Counterstrain
Basic typePassive, indirectPassive, indirect
Primary targetDiagnosed segment/tissue/AGRTender point and tenderness reduction
Starting setupNeutral/idling firstPosition of comfort/ease for tender point
ForceFacilitating force: compression, torsion, or tractionNo required added compressive force
HoldUsually 3-5 secondsClassically much longer
Exam discriminator"Neutral -> force -> ease""Tender point -> ease -> monitor tenderness"
How to recognize FPR in a vignette

If the vignette says the physician places the spinal unit in neutral, adds gentle compression, moves the segment into ease, holds briefly, and returns to neutral, pick FPR.

Q: A technique uses a tender point and patient-reported tenderness reduction as the monitor. Is this more FPR or counterstrain?

Answer

More consistent with strain-counterstrain. FPR is more often segment/AGR driven and uses a facilitating force.

W2-LO4 - Still Stepwise Approach

Technique Recipe

Define and demonstrate the stepwise approach to Still Technique.

Board-safe definition

Still technique is a combined indirect-direct method. It starts in ease, adds compression or traction, then moves through neutral toward the restrictive barrier.

  1. Diagnose the dysfunction. Name the segment/region and identify the position of ease.
  2. Start in ease. Usually exaggerate the diagnosed position. Example: C5 ERSl starts in ERSl.
  3. Add facilitating force. Compression is common; traction/distraction is allowed and may be better tolerated.
  4. Move through neutral to barrier. Carry the tissue in a smooth arc toward the direct restrictive barrier. Do not exceed physiologic ROM.
  5. Return and recheck. Return passively to neutral, repeat if needed, then recheck motion/TART.

Q: For C5 ERSl treated with Still, what is the classic treatment arc?

Answer

Start in the ease/diagnosis: C5 ERSl. Add compression. Then carry the segment toward the opposite barrier, classically toward FRSr.

W2-LO5 - Barrier Concepts

Barrier Language

Explain barrier concepts as applicable to FPR and Still Technique.

Barrier/PositionMeaningFPRStill
Position of easeDirection where tissue softens and resistance decreases.Destination after neutral and force.Starting position.
Restrictive barrierPathologic barrier reached before normal motion.Avoids it; indirect.Ends by moving toward it; direct phase.
Physiologic barrierNormal passive/active end range.Do not exceed.Do not exceed, even during direct arc.
Anatomic barrierStructural damage limit.Never a target.Never a target.
Neutral/idlingFacets neither opening nor closing; tissue has freedom to move.Starting position.Passed through during the direct arc.
One-line memory

FPR lives on the indirect side of the barrier model. Still begins indirect, then becomes direct.

Q: Which technique requires moving through neutral toward the restrictive barrier?

Answer

Still technique. FPR returns to anatomic neutral after the brief indirect hold.

W2-LO6 - Still vs Articulatory

Technique Comparison

Compare and contrast Still Technique with Articulatory Technique.

Still Technique

  • Passive combined indirect-direct technique.
  • Starts in position of ease.
  • Uses compression or traction as a facilitating force.
  • Moves through a single arc toward the barrier.

Articulatory Technique

  • Passive direct technique.
  • Moves a joint repeatedly through ROM.
  • Usually engages the restrictive barrier rhythmically.
  • Does not require starting in ease or adding the Still/FPR facilitating force.

Q: A seated thoracic technique repeatedly springs a segment at the restrictive barrier without first placing it in ease. Still or articulatory?

Answer

Articulatory. Still begins in ease and uses a facilitating force before the direct arc.

W2-LO7 - Anterior/Posterior Rib Diagnosis

Rib Diagnosis

Define and demonstrate the diagnosis of anterior and posterior rib somatic dysfunction.

Consent and draping

Mechanical rib diagnosis requires posterior and anterior palpation of the same rib. Explain why, ask permission, start from safer landmarks, and use respectful draping/hand placement.

Mechanical Rib NamePosterior Rib AngleAnterior RibHow to Confirm Same Rib
Anterior rib subluxationDeep or less prominent posteriorlyProminent anteriorlyKeep a posterior finger on the rib angle and gently move front/back until both contacts move the same rib.
Posterior rib subluxationProminent posterior rib angleDeep anterior ribCompare with adjacent ribs and reproduce local tenderness at the same rib.

Q: A rib angle sticks out posteriorly, while the anterior portion of the same rib is deep. Name the dysfunction.

Answer

Posterior rib subluxation. Posterior = prominent rib angle and deep anterior rib.

W2-LO8 - Physiologic vs Non-Physiologic Ribs

Rib Categories

Differentiate physiologic from non-physiologic rib dysfunctions.

TypeExamNamingClinical FeelWeek 2 Treatment Emphasis
Physiologic respiratory rib dysfunctionAssess rib motion during deep inhalation/exhalation over pump-handle, bucket-handle, and caliper regions.Inhalation or exhalation dysfunction.Respiratory motion restriction.Respiratory rib diagnosis/treatment from prior and ongoing rib labs.
Non-physiologic mechanical rib dysfunctionStatic positional asymmetry at posterior rib angle and anterior rib.Anterior or posterior rib subluxation.One rib is positionally stuck and often tender.Still technique using ipsilateral arm arc and rib angle monitoring.
Do not mix the names

An inhalation/exhalation dysfunction is not the same naming system as an anterior/posterior rib subluxation. The first is respiratory physiology; the second is mechanical position.

Q: A rib moves poorly with exhalation but does not have a static anterior/posterior positional asymmetry. Which category fits best?

Answer

Physiologic respiratory rib dysfunction, named by inhalation/exhalation mechanics rather than anterior/posterior subluxation.

W2-LO9 - Head/Cervical/Thoracic/Rib Screening

Screening Exam

Understand and perform the screening exam for the head, cervical, thoracic, and rib regions.

Screening is not diagnosis

The seated screen quickly finds where motion is worst. It does not replace full segmental diagnosis. After screening, fully diagnose the AGR region.

RegionPatient/Physician SetupMotion TestedWhat You Record
Head/OAPatient seated, physician cradles occiput/head.Side-slip right and left at the occiput.Side-to-side restriction. AA is usually better diagnosed supine.
CervicalStabilize head with one hand, contact each segment with the other.Translate each segment laterally R/L from upper cervicals to C7.Segment with greatest asymmetry/resistance.
ThoracicOne hand on shoulder, other just lateral to spinous processes.Inferior/medial compression through shoulder to induce segmental motion.Thoracic segment or group curve AGR.
RibsSame seated motion as thoracic, monitoring hand moves laterally to rib angles.Assess rib angle motion/prominence level by level.Rib AGR and whether ribs or thoracic spine feel worse.

Q: During screening, the thoracic spine is mildly restricted but the same level is much worse at the rib angles. What do you prioritize?

Answer

Prioritize the rib. The lab emphasized comparing spinal and rib findings and treating the most restricted finding first.

W2-LO10 - AGR

Prioritization

Identify the Area of Greatest Resistance (AGR), or worst somatic dysfunction in the above regions.

  1. Screen broadly. Move through head/OA, cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and rib angle screens quickly and symmetrically.
  2. Find the worst resistance. AGR is the area that feels most restricted, asymmetric, tender, or tissue-texture abnormal compared with neighboring regions.
  3. Compare related structures. For thorax/ribs, compare the thoracic segmental finding with the rib angle finding at the same level.
  4. Diagnose fully. Once the AGR is identified, perform the full positional diagnosis in that region instead of fully diagnosing every normal-moving level.
  5. Treat and recheck. Treat the worst finding first, then reassess. If the second finding remains, treat it next.
AGR is a workflow tool

AGR prevents wandering treatment. It tells you where the patient's body is giving the loudest diagnostic signal.

Q: Why is AGR not itself a complete diagnosis?

Answer

AGR tells you where to focus. It does not tell you the exact named somatic dysfunction until you perform positional/respiratory/mechanical diagnosis.

Q: Which regions are explicitly emphasized for Still in the Week 2 lab?

Answer

Thoracic Type 1/2, lumbar Type 2, and mechanical anterior/posterior ribs, with cervical FPR also convertible into Still by changing the order of operations.

W3-LO1 - Cervical Radiculopathy Epidemiology

Radiculopathy Bridge

Explain the epidemiology of cervical nerve root compression and identify which cervical nerve roots have the highest frequency of being compressed.

1

Frequency

Cervical radiculopathy is less common than lumbar radiculopathy. Modern summaries estimate annual adult incidence around 0.8-1.8 per 1,000 person-years.

2

Classic Study

The Rochester population study reported about 83 per 100,000 annually, with peak incidence around ages 50-54.

3

Most Common Roots

C7 is most common, followed by C6. NCBI describes C7 as more than half of cases and C6 as roughly one-quarter.

Age pattern

Younger patients more often have disc trauma/herniation. Older patients more often have degenerative foraminal narrowing from spondylosis, disc height loss, facet/uncovertebral arthrosis, and osteophytes.

Q: Which cervical root is most commonly compressed in cervical radiculopathy?

Answer

C7, followed by C6.

W3-LO2 - Spinal Root vs Peripheral Nerve

Physical Exam Differentiation

Differentiate and compare spinal nerve and peripheral nerve etiologies based on physical exams.

Exam ClueSpinal nerve/root etiologyPeripheral nerve etiology
Pain originNeck/back pain with limb radiation.Often local tunnel/entrapment pain, may not involve spine.
Sensory patternDermatomal.Named nerve distribution.
Weakness patternMyotomal; muscles sharing a root can be weak even if supplied by different peripheral nerves.Muscles supplied by one peripheral nerve are weak; same-root muscles supplied by other nerves may be spared.
ReflexesRoot-level reflex asymmetry: biceps C5/6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, patellar L4, Achilles S1.Reflexes often preserved unless the peripheral nerve contributes directly to that reflex arc.
ProvocationSpurling, shoulder abduction relief, SLR/slump/femoral stretch can reproduce root symptoms.Tinel/Phalen/cubital tunnel compression/fibular head compression reproduce local nerve symptoms.

Q: A patient has wrist/hand paresthesia with positive Phalen but no neck pain, normal Spurling, and median nerve sensory distribution. Root or peripheral nerve?

Answer

More consistent with peripheral median nerve entrapment, not a cervical root pattern.

W3-LO3 - Nerve Irritation Symptoms

Clinical Features

Explain the signs and symptoms of spinal nerve irritation (pain, paresthesia, weakness).

Irritation -> pain; dysfunction -> deficit

A nerve root can be irritated before it fails. Pain and paresthesia may appear first; objective weakness/reflex loss suggests more functional compromise.

Symptom/SignWhat It MeansExample
PainNociceptive/inflammatory root irritation, often sharp, electric, radiating.Neck pain radiating to middle finger in C7 pattern.
Paresthesia/numbnessSensory fiber irritation or dysfunction.Thumb/lateral forearm symptoms suggest C6; dorsum/middle finger suggests C7.
WeaknessMotor fiber dysfunction in a myotome.C7 can weaken triceps; L5 can weaken dorsiflexion/great toe extension.
Reflex changeObjective root-level neurologic sign.Depressed triceps reflex supports C7; decreased Achilles supports S1.

Q: Pain plus paresthesia without objective weakness may be described as what?

Answer

Radiculitis is often used for root irritation/inflammation without objective neurologic deficit.

W3-LO4 - Radiculitis vs Radiculopathy vs Myelopathy

Definitions

Differentiate between radiculitis, radiculopathy, and myelopathy.

TermPrimary ProblemTypical FindingsClinical Response
RadiculitisInflamed/irritated nerve root.Radiating pain and paresthesia; no clear objective weakness/reflex loss.Conservative care and monitor for progression.
RadiculopathyNerve-root dysfunction from compression/inflammation/ischemia.Dermatomal sensory change, myotomal weakness, and/or reflex loss.Root-level localization; imaging/electrodiagnostics if severe, unclear, progressive, or persistent.
MyelopathySpinal cord dysfunction.Gait instability, hand clumsiness, hyperreflexia, clonus, Hoffman/Babinski, possible bowel/bladder symptoms.Red flag. Escalate evaluation rather than treating as a simple segmental/root issue.

Q: A patient has neck pain, hand clumsiness, brisk reflexes, positive Hoffman sign, and gait instability. Radiculopathy or myelopathy?

Answer

Myelopathy. Upper motor neuron signs and gait change point to spinal cord involvement.

W3-LO5 - Spondylosis and Spondyloarthropathy

Pathophysiology

Define and explain the pathophysiology of spondylosis and spondyloarthropathy.

Spondylosis

Degenerative spine change: disc dehydration/height loss, annular fissuring, osteophytes, facet arthrosis, uncovertebral arthrosis in the cervical spine, and foraminal/canal narrowing.

  • Can be asymptomatic.
  • Can cause radiculopathy if neuroforamen/lateral recess narrows.
  • Can contribute to stenosis or myelopathy when canal compromise affects the cord.

Spondyloarthropathy

Inflammatory axial/entheseal disease rather than wear-and-tear degeneration. Think sacroiliitis, enthesitis, inflammatory back pain, HLA-B27 association, and links with psoriasis, uveitis, or IBD.

  • Morning stiffness and pain improve with exercise.
  • Alternating buttock pain is a clue.
  • Not a single-root dermatomal pattern.

Q: A 27-year-old has insidious low back pain, morning stiffness, alternating buttock pain, and improves with exercise. Spondylosis or spondyloarthropathy?

Answer

Spondyloarthropathy, because the pattern is inflammatory rather than degenerative/mechanical.

W3-LO6 - Cervical/Lumbar Differentials

Differential Diagnosis

Compare, contrast, explain and identify cervical and lumbar findings such as spinal stenosis, cervical or lumbar disc herniation, spondylosis, spondylolysis, spondylolisthesis, spondyloarthropathy, psoas syndrome, piriformis syndrome, bursitis.

ConditionPathophysiologyTypical FindingsKey Differentiator
Cervical/lumbar disc herniationNucleus/disc material causes chemical irritation and mechanical root compression.Radicular pain, dermatomal sensory change, myotomal weakness, reflex loss; lumbar symptoms often worsen with sitting/cough/sneeze.A common cause of true radiculopathy.
Spinal stenosisCanal/lateral recess/foraminal narrowing from disc bulge, ligamentum flavum, facet hypertrophy, osteophytes, or spondylolisthesis.Neurogenic claudication, worse standing/walking/extension, relief with flexion.Often multi-root or bilateral/asymmetric rather than one clean root.
SpondylosisDegenerative disc/facet/uncovertebral changes.Axial pain/stiffness, decreased ROM, possible foraminal narrowing.Imaging degeneration must correlate with exam; many findings are incidental.
SpondylolysisPars interarticularis stress defect/fracture.Extension-related low back pain, often adolescent/athlete.Usually local mechanical pain unless slip/stenosis affects roots.
SpondylolisthesisVertebral slippage, often isthmic or degenerative.Mechanical low back pain, step-off, hamstring tightness; radicular symptoms if foramina narrow.X-ray/MRI shows slippage; L5-S1 is classic for isthmic, L4-L5 for degenerative.
SpondyloarthropathyInflammatory axial/enthesis disease.Morning stiffness, improvement with exercise, SI pain, uveitis/psoriasis/IBD history.Inflammatory/systemic pattern, not dermatomal root deficit.
Psoas syndromeIliopsoas tendon/muscle/bursa irritation or overuse.Anterior hip/groin pain, worse hip extension or resisted hip flexion, possible snapping.Local hip/psoas provocation; radiation usually does not extend below knee.
Piriformis syndromeSciatic nerve irritation near piriformis.Buttock pain radiating posterior leg, worse sitting, FAIR/Pace/Freiberg provocation.Sciatica-like with negative spine/root workup.
Trochanteric bursitis/GTPSLateral hip bursal/tendinous pain around greater trochanter.Lateral hip tenderness, pain lying on affected side, stairs worsen.No dermatomal sensory loss, root reflex loss, or myotomal weakness.
Red flags change the plan

Escalate for progressive motor deficit, myelopathic signs, bowel/bladder dysfunction, saddle anesthesia, fever, cancer/infection risk, significant trauma, fracture/instability, or cervical vascular symptoms.

Q: Shopping-cart posture relieves leg symptoms triggered by standing/walking. Which lumbar diagnosis rises?

Answer

Lumbar spinal stenosis with neurogenic claudication. Flexion opens the canal/foramina relative to extension.

Week 2 OMM - High-Yield One-Pager

Condensed by learning objective. Use this as a final pass after reading the full sections.

W2-LO1 - FPR Stepwise Approach

FPR = passive, indirect technique: segment/tissue placed in neutral/idling, a facilitating force is added, then moved into its position of ease.

  1. Diagnose & monitor - name the dysfunction, keep a palpating hand on the segment/tender tissue/AGR.
  2. Neutral/idling - facets neither opened nor closed (cervical: flex down to the level).
  3. Facilitating force - usually gentle compression/torsion; use traction if compression not tolerated.
  4. Move into ease - position segment into its freedom of motion (indirect component).
  5. Hold, return, recheck - hold 3-5 sec, passively return to anatomic neutral, repeat if needed, reassess TART/motion.
W2-LO2 - FPR/Still Indications, Contraindications, MOA

Indications: somatic dysfunction with restricted motion, TART, or local AGR; hypertonic muscles (superficial/group curve or deep/segmental restriction); fascial restrictions and limited-ROM patients who tolerate low-force positioning.

Contraindications/cautions: patient cannot tolerate the position or refuses; recent trauma, unstable joint pathology, severe osteoporosis, malignancy, infection, severe rheumatologic disease, congenital instability/malformation, or stenosis. Region-specific: cervical radiculopathy is a caution; hip replacement can contraindicate some lumbar leg-sweep setups.

TechniqueProposed MOAPractical Implication
FPRShortens involved muscle spindles, decreases gamma efferent gain, lowers Ia afferent excitation, reduces extrafusal muscle tone.Use relaxed/passive positioning - shorten and quiet tone, don't fight it.
StillSame proposed neurophysiologic relaxation, then adds a direct mobilizing arc through neutral toward the barrier.Start gentle/indirect, then carry tissue into the direct phase while staying within physiologic ROM.

Force choice is clinical reasoning: compression is common, but if it worsens symptoms or jams the region, use traction/distraction or a smaller arc.

W2-LO3 - FPR vs Strain-Counterstrain
FeatureFPRStrain-Counterstrain
Basic typePassive, indirectPassive, indirect
Primary targetDiagnosed segment/tissue/AGRTender point and tenderness reduction
Starting setupNeutral/idling firstPosition of comfort/ease for the tender point
ForceFacilitating force: compression, torsion, or tractionNo required added compressive force
HoldUsually 3-5 secondsClassically much longer
Exam discriminator"Neutral → force → ease""Tender point → ease → monitor tenderness"

Vignette tell: if the physician places the spinal unit in neutral, adds gentle compression, moves into ease, holds briefly, then returns to neutral → FPR. If the monitor is a tender point and reported tenderness reduction → strain-counterstrain.

W2-LO4 - Still Stepwise Approach

Still technique = combined indirect-direct method: starts in ease, adds compression/traction, then moves through neutral toward the restrictive barrier.

  1. Diagnose - name the segment/region, identify the position of ease.
  2. Start in ease - usually exaggerate the diagnosed position (e.g., C5 ERSl starts in ERSl).
  3. Add facilitating force - compression common; traction/distraction allowed and may be better tolerated.
  4. Move through neutral to barrier - smooth arc toward the direct restrictive barrier, staying within physiologic ROM.
  5. Return and recheck - passively return to neutral, repeat if needed, recheck motion/TART.

Example: C5 ERSl → start in ERSl → compress → carry toward opposite barrier, classically FRSr.

One-line memory: FPR lives on the indirect side of the barrier model. Still begins indirect, then becomes direct.

W2-LO6 - Still vs Articulatory

Vignette tell: repeated springing at the restrictive barrier without first placing the joint in ease → articulatory. Starting in ease with a facilitating force before a single direct arc → Still.

W2-LO7 - Anterior/Posterior Rib Diagnosis
  • Anterior rib subluxation: deep/less-prominent posterior rib angle + prominent anterior rib.
  • Posterior rib subluxation: prominent posterior rib angle + deep anterior rib.
  • Confirm it's the same rib front and back: keep a posterior finger on the rib angle and move the anterior contact until both move together; compare with adjacent ribs and reproduce local tenderness.
  • Requires posterior + anterior palpation - explain why, get consent, start from safer landmarks, use respectful draping/hand placement.
W2-LO8 - Physiologic vs Non-Physiologic Ribs
TypeExam/NamingClinical FeelTreatment Emphasis
Physiologic (respiratory)Assess rib motion during deep inhale/exhale over pump-handle, bucket-handle, caliper regions; named inhalation or exhalation dysfunction.Respiratory motion restriction.Respiratory rib diagnosis/treatment from rib labs.
Non-physiologic (mechanical)Static positional asymmetry at posterior rib angle and anterior rib; named anterior or posterior rib subluxation.One rib positionally stuck and often tender.Still technique using ipsilateral arm arc and rib angle monitoring.

Do not mix naming systems: inhalation/exhalation dysfunction is respiratory physiology; anterior/posterior subluxation is mechanical position.

W2-LO9 - Head/Cervical/Thoracic/Rib Screening

Screening finds where motion is worst quickly - it is not full diagnosis. After screening, fully diagnose the AGR region.

RegionSetupMotion TestedWhat You Record
Head/OAPatient seated, physician cradles occiput/head.Side-slip right and left at the occiput.Side-to-side restriction (AA better diagnosed supine).
CervicalStabilize head with one hand, contact each segment with the other.Translate each segment laterally R/L from upper cervicals to C7.Segment with greatest asymmetry/resistance.
ThoracicOne hand on shoulder, other just lateral to spinous processes.Inferior/medial compression through shoulder to induce segmental motion.Thoracic segment or group curve AGR.
RibsSame seated setup, monitoring hand moves laterally to rib angles.Assess rib angle motion/prominence level by level.Rib AGR and whether ribs or thoracic spine feel worse.
W2-LO10 - AGR
  1. Screen broadly - move through head/OA, cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and rib angle screens quickly and symmetrically.
  2. Find the worst resistance - AGR is the area most restricted, asymmetric, tender, or tissue-texture abnormal vs. neighboring regions.
  3. Compare related structures - for thorax/ribs, compare the thoracic segmental finding with the rib angle finding at the same level.
  4. Diagnose fully - once AGR is found, fully diagnose that region instead of every normal-moving level.
  5. Treat and recheck - treat the worst finding first, reassess, then treat the next finding if it remains.

AGR is a workflow tool: it tells you where to focus, not the exact named somatic dysfunction until positional/respiratory/mechanical diagnosis is performed.

W2-LO11 - Regional FPR/Still Treatment
RegionDiagnosis RuleFPR ApplicationStill Application
OAOpposite sidebending/rotation; named OA F/E Sx Ry.Neutralize OA, add gentle force, move into OA ease for 3-5 sec.Start in OA ease, add force, carry toward opposite barrier.
AAPrimarily rotation; named AA Rr or AA Rl.Neutral upper cervical setup, gentle force, rotate toward ease briefly.Start rotated toward ease, add force, carry toward restrictive rotation barrier.
Lower cervicalC2-C7 usually Type 2; sidebending and rotation same side.Flex to neutral/idling level, compress, move into ease (e.g. C5 ERSl → neutral, compress, ease ERSl).Start in ease/diagnosis, compress, move opposite (e.g. C5 ERSl → toward FRSr).
Thoracic Type 1Neutral group curve; rotation and sidebending opposite.Reduce kyphosis to neutral, compress, move group curve into freedom.Start in group-curve ease, compress through torso, carry toward opposite barrier.
Thoracic Type 2Single segment F/E with rotation and sidebending same side.Sit up to neutral, compress, position F/E + S/R into ease.Start in diagnosis/ease, compress, move to opposite F/E and opposite S/R.
Lumbar Type 2Supine; prominent TP gives rotation. Adduction = flexion, abduction = extension.Conceptual only - Week 2 lab emphasizes Still for lumbar.Use lower extremity: start in flexion or extension ease, add compression/traction, sweep through opposite arc.
Anterior/posterior ribAnterior = deep angle/prominent anterior. Posterior = prominent angle/deep anterior.Not the Week 2 emphasis for mechanical ribs.Monitor rib angle, find ipsilateral arm ease, compress toward rib, move arm through opposite arc to barrier.

Regions explicitly emphasized for Still in the Week 2 lab: thoracic Type 1/2, lumbar Type 2, and mechanical anterior/posterior ribs, with cervical FPR also convertible into Still by changing the order of operations.

W3-LO1 - Cervical Radiculopathy Epidemiology
  • C7 most common cervical root, then C6.
  • Root = dermatome/myotome/reflex; peripheral nerve = named nerve distribution.
  • Myelopathy = cord signs and escalation.
  • Differentiate disc, stenosis, spondylosis, inflammatory disease, and hip/buttock mimics.
